rv.q: It’s a magnificent piece of theatre: richly funny, deeply moving and superbly acted by an outstanding ensemble led by Brendan Gleeson.
It’s an endlessly rewarding evening that proves McPherson’s play is built to last.
A total must-see for anyone who loves the art of storytelling.
And what better actor to pop the cork on such intoxicating liquor than the inscrutable, bearlike Gleeson?

The scenario is old-fashioned in its simplicity but enables a drama of breathtaking craft, tilting line by line between levity and profundity, the far-fetched and the truth, superstition and faith – remarkable given McPherson was only 25 when he wrote it.

And its carefully interwoven strands of the mundane and the supernatural give this play an enduring strength – one that tugs audiences into this little tavern, long after they’ve called time on other plays of its vintage.

But an accomplished group of actors can find depths in glances and silences. Whether or not The Weir…really is an all-time classic, as many insist it is, this production, directed by McPherson, is worth catching to see Brendan Gleeson give a display that is as unyielding and enigmatic as a neolithic rock carving.
The play’s rolling rhythm beautifully evokes an atmosphere of loss and regret like a low throb beneath the crotchety camaraderie that also defines these men who have forged connections across a bar.
This production, almost 30 years on, is quite perfect.
It is a staggeringly good production of a play that is already a classic, that does so much by seeming to do nothing.
A touching play, a timeless play played with perfect timing, The Weir is a must-see. Five-star quality all round.
Nothing obscures the fact that this is the Irish classic so many recent comers have wanted, and failed, to be.
While one can admire the craftsmanship of both script and performance, the production ultimately struggles to sustain dramatic energy across its running time.
I can't help thinking, despite some excellent performances (Brendan Gleeson's Jack is especially convincing here), it was a bit too leisurely paced and introspective.
This is a superb revival of a modern classic, made all the more special by McPherson’s own hand at the helm.
A testament to the art of storytelling, both in the stories told throughout the play and the play itself, The Weir is one story you’ll want to hear in full.
This top-notch revival is a timely reminder that theatre need not shout to be powerful.
I found the delivery of the stories to be mixed in quality and was not always sure that they always found their mark.
It’s the perfect time of year for this atmospheric tale to work its magic not least when Valerie decides to tell a tale of her own.

cn.t: McPherson's 1997 masterpiece proves timeless in this spellbinding revival, with Brendan Gleeson's West End debut anchoring a pitch-perfect ensemble. Critics hail the atmospheric pub drama's quiet power, lyrical storytelling, and emotional depth.
